prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an address such as https://www.example.com/products into a browser and press Enter, the browser first has to work out what you actually asked for. It parses the string into a scheme (https), a host (www.example.com), an optional port (443 is implied by https), a path, and any query or fragment. It also checks a few local sources before touching the network. If the host is on the browser's HSTS list, which records sites that must only be reached over HTTPS, the browser will refuse to fall back to plain HTTP. It also looks in its HTTP cache. If it holds a fresh copy of the resource, as allowed by the Cache-Control or Expires headers from an earlier visit, it can render immediately and no network request happens at all. Assume the cache misses.

The browser now needs an IP address, because the network routes packets to addresses, not names. It checks its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system's resolver, which checks its own cache and the hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the OS sends a query, usually over UDP port 53, to a recursive resolver. That is typically run by your ISP, your router, or a public provider, and some setups use DNS over HTTPS instead. The recursive resolver does the legwork if it has no cached answer. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and finally asks one of them for the address of www.example.com. The answer may be a CNAME pointing to another name, which has to be resolved in turn, and it carries a time-to-live telling every cache along the way how long it may be reused. Modern browsers may request both A (IPv4) and AAAA (IPv6) records and race the connections, which is sometimes called Happy Eyeballs, so a broken IPv6 route does not leave you waiting. Many sites also publish HTTPS records that advertise supported protocols, which can save a round trip later.

With an IP address in hand, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443. TCP provides an ordered, reliable byte stream on top of unreliable packets, and it begins with a three-way handshake. The client sends a SYN, the server answers with a SYN-ACK, and the client replies with an ACK. This costs one full round trip before any application data can flow, so physical distance matters here: a server on another continent can add well over a hundred milliseconds. If the browser already has an open connection to the same origin from a previous request, it can reuse that connection and skip this step entirely, which is one reason connection pooling and keep-alive matter. Along the way your packets cross your local network, a NAT router that rewrites your private address to a public one, and many routers owned by different networks. Each router forwards the packet to the next hop based on its routing table. Content delivery networks shorten this journey by answering DNS with the address of a nearby edge server rather than the origin machine.

Next comes the TLS handshake, which is what turns HTTP into HTTPS. Its job is to let the browser verify it is talking to the real owner of the domain and to establish keys for encrypting everything that follows. In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello listing the protocol versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, a key share for a Diffie-Hellman style key exchange, and the Server Name Indication extension containing the hostname. SNI matters because one IP address may host many sites, and the server needs to know which certificate to present. The ALPN extension in the same message lists the application protocols the client can speak, such as h2 for HTTP/2 and http/1.1. The server replies with its own key share and the chosen cipher suite, and both sides can now derive shared secret keys without ever sending the secret itself. The server then sends, already encrypted, its certificate chain and a signature proving it holds the matching private key, followed by a Finished message.

The browser validates that certificate chain before trusting it. It checks that the leaf certificate covers the requested hostname through its Subject Alternative Name entries, that the dates are valid, and that the chain leads through one or more intermediate certificates to a root authority already present in the operating system or browser trust store. It checks every signature along the chain and may check revocation status through stapled OCSP responses or compiled-in revocation lists. If anything fails, the browser shows the full-page warning you have probably seen rather than continuing. If everything passes, the browser sends its own Finished message and the connection is secured. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this, where TLS 1.2 needed two. If you have visited the site recently, session resumption or 0-RTT can shorten it further, though 0-RTT data has replay risks, so it is restricted to safe requests. Sites using HTTP/3 take a different route entirely: it runs over QUIC on UDP, which folds the transport and TLS handshakes into a single exchange, and the browser learns about it through an Alt-Svc header or an HTTPS DNS record.

Only now does the browser send the actual request. Under HTTP/1.1 this is plain text inside the encrypted channel, a request line such as GET /products HTTP/1.1, followed by headers like Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding, and any cookies stored for that domain, then a blank line. Under HTTP/2 the same information is carried as compressed binary frames, so many requests can share a single connection at once. The browser may also attach cache validators such as If-None-Match, so the server can answer with a tiny 304 Not Modified instead of resending a page the browser already holds.

The request travels through the encrypted tunnel to the server's side, where it often hits a load balancer or reverse proxy before reaching an application server. That layer may terminate TLS, check a cache, apply rate limits, route by path, and finally hand the request to your application code. The application might query a database, call other services, and render a page, and all of that processing time is added to the wait. When the response is ready, the server writes a status line, headers, and the beginning of the body. The moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser is the time to first byte, or TTFB. It is the sum of everything above: DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, request transit, server processing, and the return trip. That is why developers watch each phase separately in the browser's network panel, since each one has different fixes: caching DNS, using a CDN, enabling keep-alive and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, or making the backend itself faster.
